format: Two 20-minute slots: approximately 15 minutes of presentation and 5 minutes of discussion, with optional backup slides

conceptual.title:
Agency across
scales
conceptual.subtitle:
Boundaries, representations,
and the capacity to act
conceptual.notes: Opening, about 45 seconds. I want to connect our work on computational mechanics and neural representations to a question about agency: when do interacting components form a larger unit that can usefully be described as acting? My proposal is to approach this through interfaces and the distinctions they preserve. This is a conceptual argument with a developing formal specification. I will distinguish established source results, observations reported in the group's drafts, and my proposed extensions. The second talk will use AI islands as a concrete organizational test case. The cover is an AI-generated textile metaphor for organization across scales, not a measured network or scientific result.

conceptual.title: The organizing question
conceptual.statement: Which distinctions must survive a boundary for a system to respond effectively?
conceptual.body:
A predictive pattern is a starting point.
An agency claim also needs an account of action and regulation.
conceptual.notes: About 75 seconds. A system can be composed of many interacting parts and still have a useful higher-level description. Think of a team that can revise a plan even as the people doing particular jobs change. The interesting question is what makes that description earn its place. I suggest looking at what enters and leaves the proposed unit, and what distinctions remain available when it must respond to a changed condition. This connects prediction to agency while leaving the criteria for agency open to discussion. I am using meaningful organization to mean organization that supports an explanatory and task-relevant description. This does not yet settle semantic meaning, consciousness, moral standing, or legitimate authority. This slide states the proposed synthesis, rather than a result from a single paper.

conceptual.title: Process, representation, and authority
rows: What information supports prediction and response?
Who can decide, intervene, or challenge?
conceptual.caption: A simpler predictive model can help understanding. Effective authority requires separate evidence.
conceptual.notes: About 90 seconds. These distinctions are the backbone of both talks. First, there is the actual interacting process, including its communications and environmental effects. Second, there is an observer's representation, which might be a Bayesian belief, a neural activation, or a human-facing summary. Third, in organizations, there are rights and permissions over decisions. Hiding an exchange from an observer changes the second object. Removing the exchange changes the first. Giving a person an enforceable veto changes the third. If we change all of them at once, we cannot tell why an arrangement helped or failed. This is a modeling choice adopted for this project. It also prevents a neural observation about low-dimensional representations from silently becoming a claim about human power.

conceptual.title: A higher level with a description of its own
items: Does the macro history retain the predictive information available from the micro history?
Under the paper’s conditions, macro states can preserve a coherent portion of the underlying computation.
The retained distinctions must matter for the behavior we want to explain.
conceptual.caption: Existing closure framework plus a proposed requirement of task relevance
conceptual.notes: About 90 seconds. Software in the Natural World gives a precise language for higher-level organization. Compare predicting the future macroprocess from its own history with predicting it from the underlying micro history. Informational closure says the latter adds no predictive information. The paper defines causal-state and computational forms of closure as well, with specific relationships between them. The informational-to-computational implication discussed here uses spatial coarse-graining. I would add task relevance when selecting a description for our project, because a constant macrovariable could be closed without explaining anything useful. Closure across levels is compatible with ongoing exchange across an agent-environment boundary. Sources: Rosas et al., Software in the Natural World, arXiv:2402.09090v2, PDF pp. 3–8, especially the counterfactual qualifications on pp. 4 and 6. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09090v2

conceptual.title: Perception–action boundaries
rows: Environment history that improves prediction of the system’s next state, given its own history
System history that improves prediction of the environment’s next state, given its own history
conceptual.caption: Causal blankets exist for every bipartition. The boundary still needs justification.
conceptual.notes: About 90 seconds. Causal Blankets starts with a candidate division into a system and its environment. It then constructs minimal dynamical sufficient statistics in each direction. These supply sensory and active sides of an informational interface. They can summarize a history, so they need not look like a physical membrane. The existence result is very general: each bipartition has such a blanket. That means existence alone cannot tell us which boundary is the agent. We should compare candidate divisions at a specified timescale, ask which make a useful description, and test proposed channels. The stronger trajectory-independence result requires factorisable dynamics. The paper explicitly warns that partial observation limits counterfactual guarantees. Source: Rosas et al., Causal Blankets, arXiv:2008.12568v2, PDF pp. 3–7. https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.12568v2

conceptual.title: A working account of agency
items: A recognizable unit and interface over the task’s timescale
Outputs that change relevant environmental outcomes
Responses that maintain or recover a specified target under change
An explanation that improves on a stated component-level alternative
conceptual.caption: Proposed graded criteria, open to revision
conceptual.notes: About 90 seconds. This is the additional conceptual commitment I want to discuss. I would require evidence of an organized unit that persists over a relevant timescale, effective action on its surroundings, and regulation through feedback. To justify a claim at a collective scale, I would also compare the explanatory value of that collective description with a specified alternative using components separately. These are working criteria, not necessary and sufficient conditions proven by the source papers. A thermostat may satisfy a minimal form of regulation. Planning, learning, and revising goals would support stronger claims, without making them mandatory for every minimal agent. We also need to state the target being maintained and avoid inventing a goal after observing a regularity. Agency remains separate from consciousness and from any right to decide for others.

conceptual.title: The question can recur at different scales
rows: Does a selective intervention change a specific response across contexts?
Does feedback restore a target after a disturbance?
Can the group revise a plan when evidence or membership changes?
conceptual.caption: A shared research question does not establish identical mechanisms across these settings.
conceptual.notes: About 75 seconds. These are illustrations of how a question can recur, not evidence that the three systems instantiate the same mathematical model. In a neural system, we might perturb a candidate representation and ask what downstream behavior changes. In a controller, we might introduce an environmental disturbance. In a team, we might change the evidence or a participant and ask whether a coordinated response persists. An intervention-sensitive representation inside a predictor still does not automatically qualify as an agent. We would need the additional properties from the previous slide. The variables, feasible interventions, and outcomes change across domains. So the cross-scale connection is initially methodological: compare interfaces and responses. A stronger claim that a result transfers requires a specific mapping and evidence that the relevant mechanisms persist.

conceptual.title: What the neural draft reports
rows: A model can represent a useful decomposition
Interventions can test causal use of that representation
Less observed detail can make predictive representation more demanding
conceptual.caption: Small transformers on synthetic feedback processes. Reported draft results, not a replication here.
conceptual.notes: About 90 seconds. The feedback draft gives the most concrete link to our group's work. In small transformers trained on known interacting processes, it reports decodable per-factor beliefs, patching experiments that move predictions toward counterfactual references, and examples where omitting an observed stream raises effective rank. The patching evidence matters: it goes beyond a decoding correlation. But we should keep the scope explicit. The evidence concerns synthetic tasks with known reference beliefs. The factors are what the predictor represents, which is different from discovering autonomous agents inside the predictor. Also, presentation dimension, belief-cloud PCA rank, and neural effective rank are different quantities. I am omitting headline dimensional numbers to keep that distinction clear. Source: supplied Beliefs in Feedback Loops draft, PDF pp. 4–9, 36–38, archived 10 November 2026, SHA256 prefix 52e8f0c44838.

conceptual.title: Tests that would strengthen the connection
items: Matched probes at initialization and after training, plus selective interventions
Compare compact factors, nonlinear reconstruction, and access to earlier messages
Test changed policies, reveal orders, and correlated priors
conceptual.caption: Proposed next experiments
conceptual.notes: About 90 seconds. The next experiments should build on the draft's existing intervention tests. First, compare decoding across layers and training stages with matched decoder capacity. The draft already reports substantial decoding at random initialization, so high decoding alone is not the conclusion. Second, ask whether targeted edits have the intended effect without broad leakage into other factors. Third, compare ways the network could avoid storing a large joint table. Simon's notes describe factored storage with nonlinear reconstruction and using earlier tokens. Those are important alternative explanations. Finally, test new policy and reveal-order combinations and priors with initial dependence. The unverified propositions and preliminary approximations in Simon's draft remain unverified. Sources: feedback draft, p. 5 and pp. 24–26; Iliad_project_notes-1.pdf, pp. 7–10. These experiments have not been run in this repository.

conceptual.title: Routine prediction can miss a useful correction
conceptual.caption: Constructed example: a Z-only report incurs 0.05 excess expected loss overall.
conceptual.notes: About 2 minutes. This is the repository's checked constructed example. Z and R are independent fair bits. Routine behavior sets the next Z to one minus Z. Switching sets the next Z to R and adds a loss of 0.2. Loss is one minus the next Z, plus that switching cost. A report that contains only Z therefore predicts the routine Z trajectory perfectly. But when Z equals one, the best action depends on R. With only Z, the expected switching loss is 0.7, so the best rule switches. It loses 0.2 in the R-equals-zero case and loses nothing relative to full information in the other three equally likely cases. Hence overall excess loss is 0.05. Ask the group briefly which missing fact changes the choice. This is a one-step decision result, not an organizational experiment and not a counterexample to an action-complete transducer. Source: output/pdf/verify_counterexample.py, exact enumeration, rechecked 18 November 2026.
conceptual.body:
Independent fair bits Z, R. Loss = 1 − Z′ + switching cost.
Routine: Z′ = 1 − Z. Switch: Z′ = R, with cost 0.2.

conceptual.title: An interface that supports correction
conceptual.statement: Histories merged by a report should remain sufficiently alike under the corrective policies we actually allow.
conceptual.body:
Specify the action set, outcomes, horizon, and tolerance.
Measure decision loss and human effort separately.
conceptual.notes: About 90 seconds. This is the formal direction, phrased without committing to a final theorem. If a report makes two histories look identical, we want to know whether those histories have similar consequences under feasible future policies. We must fix what a policy can observe, which actions it can take, the future horizon, and the outcomes we care about. The criterion in the appendix uses distances between outcome distributions. It is deliberately strong and may be more than we need to preserve one particular decision, so task-specific decision loss also matters. This is not a new invention of action-conditioned sufficiency. AI in a Vat and the epsilon-transducer literature already treat interfaces over action sequences. The proposed extension concerns human-usable reports and constrained correction rights. Source: Rosas, Boyd and Baltieri, AI in a Vat, archived 38-page snapshot, PDF pp. 4–6 and 10. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04608

conceptual.title: The research claim to discuss
conceptual.statement: Interfaces can connect the study of predictive organization to the study of effective action.
items: Which candidate partition earns its explanatory role?
What evidence distinguishes regulation from a regular pattern?
Which distinctions must remain available for correction?
conceptual.notes: Reserve about 5 minutes for discussion, adjusting earlier slides to fit the 20-minute slot. My claim is a research connection rather than a unified theory already proved. Computational mechanics supplies candidate representations and boundaries. Neural experiments can test their implementation and use. The agency proposal adds regulation and effective action. The organizational extension asks whose ability to correct decisions survives the interface. Invite objections to the proposed agency criteria first, then ask what the smallest decisive experiment would be. If the discussion turns to human authority, bridge to the second talk: even a representation that preserves the right distinctions needs an institution that lets a person act on them. The two formal source papers do not establish moral standing or legitimate decision authority.

conceptual.title: Backup: a light formal specification
items: Y_next is independent of X_past given A and Y_past
Same report implies outcome laws within ε for every feasible policy σ
conceptual.caption: Fixed model, histories, report updates, horizon, outcome vector, and policy family
conceptual.notes: Optional backup, outside the timed core. The closure expression is shorthand for the relevant future horizons, with well-defined information quantities and the source's process assumptions. The directional interface also requires A to be a function of X's history, with minimality if constructing the minimal statistic. Reverse X and Y for the sensory direction. For the proposed report requirement, define Q^sigma(.|h) using the controlled generator initialized after history h and a common policy sigma implementable through the stated information and actions. Require sup over sigma of total-variation distance between Q^sigma(.|h) and Q^sigma(.|h') to be at most epsilon whenever tau(h)=tau(h'). A finite test establishes only tested coverage. This is a proposed sufficient-information criterion, not a new theorem or an agency definition. See the companion essay for the full specification and references.

organizational.title:
AI islands and
human control
organizational.subtitle:
A design hypothesis
for human–AI organizations
organizational.notes: Opening, about 45 seconds. I want to build on Alec's islands proposal and ask what it would actually require in an organization. The guiding outcome is whether people can notice a consequential problem and change the decision. I will describe a concrete workflow, identify what the conceptual connection supports, and propose comparisons that could favor either islands or a less restrictive arrangement. This is a design hypothesis and proposed research program. No human pilot has been run. The cover image is an AI-generated textile metaphor used as a background, not a diagram of a measured system.

organizational.title: Alec’s islands proposal
items: People retain direct relationships and opportunities to deliberate.
AI collaboration passes through interfaces people can inspect.
Prevent direct AI messages, or permit them with effective review?
organizational.caption: The meeting emphasizes separation. The written draft also considers observable communication.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. The island metaphor reverses a picture in which people depend on a central AI while losing direct relationships with each other. In the meeting, Alec proposes people communicating directly and AIs communicating through people. The supplied written draft also makes observability and understanding central, allowing an interpretation in which a direct channel could remain if it is effectively reviewed. I want to keep these variants distinct because their practical implications differ. The meeting also raises beneficial coordination, shared priors, and indirect communication. Those objections belong in the design. We should not treat the transcript as independent verification of technical claims or external incidents. Sources: The Dimensional Balance of Power, working draft dated 26 October 2026, sections 5–6; local numbered meeting transcript, lines 107–136 and 141–169. The exact meeting date is not established.

organizational.title: The conceptual link
organizational.statement: What people can observe may change the cost of understanding an interacting system.
organizational.body:
The feedback draft supplies a mechanism to investigate.
Human control still depends on usable information and effective authority.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. Under the feedback draft's specified operators and an existing product-form belief, updates preserve a factored representation. Its synthetic examples also show how marginalizing an observed stream can make predictive representation more demanding. This gives us a reason to study communication interfaces. It does not directly establish a policy. Hiding a message from an observer leaves the message operating in the generator, whereas banning or rerouting it changes the process. Nor does a lower-dimensional predictor automatically become understandable to a person. We need an empirical bridge from predictive representation to usable review, and another from review to effective action. Sources: Beliefs in Feedback Loops, PDF pp. 4–9, 24–26 and 36–38. These are reported draft findings, not an organizational trial or a replication in this repository.

organizational.title: Five choices inside an island design
rows: Make an existing exchange available to a reviewer
Gate, remove, or reroute an exchange
Summarize while preserving access to dissent and evidence
Require approval before a specified commitment
Decide whose interests and objections count
organizational.caption: Each choice changes a different part of the model or institution.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. These choices make the proposal concrete. Observation is what the reviewer can access. Communication is how the participants actually exchange information. Reporting is the representation offered to the reviewer. Execution rights determine who can commit an action. Objectives and standing specify the values and people the arrangement serves. A shared writable document belongs in the communication specification even if nobody sends a chat message. Timing belongs in the first four choices because evidence that arrives after an irreversible action cannot support that correction. If all five change at once, an outcome difference is difficult to interpret. This separation is the project's proposed modeling discipline, informed by the source distinctions between observation and generator changes. It is not a claim that information theory chooses legitimate objectives.

organizational.title: A fictional research-budget decision
items: Reviews proposals in a private workspace
Checks sources, uncertainty, and dissent before sharing a report
Proposes an allocation from the approved material
Inspects objections and authorizes the final allocation
organizational.caption: Illustrative pilot. No real funds move. Direct human discussion remains available.
organizational.notes: About 2 minutes. Here is one concrete island condition. An evidence assistant and a planning assistant support people allocating a fictional budget. The evidence assistant works in a private workspace. Its human partner checks a structured handoff before it becomes an input to the planner. The handoff includes sources, uncertainty, and dissenting evidence, with access to the originals. Shared writable tools are restricted or explicitly accounted for. Humans can talk directly and ask for revisions. A designated human authorizes the final decision. Now introduce a missed constraint affecting a small proposal. Can someone recover the evidence and change the allocation before authorization? That is the test. Reviewers may also lose information or become a bottleneck. A logged collaboration condition with identical final execution rights is therefore an essential comparator. This workflow is our proposed example, not Alec's fully specified protocol and not an experiment already conducted.

organizational.title: Control as an observable sequence
items: The relevant information arrives before commitment.
A person recognizes the consequential problem.
The person can challenge the plan and request a change.
The intervention changes the outcome before the relevant harm.
organizational.caption: Measure failures at each step, along with unnecessary vetoes, effort, and task quality.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. This is our proposed operational account of control. It is deliberately more demanding than showing a human in a workflow diagram. First, relevant information must arrive in time. Second, someone must understand enough to recognize the problem. Third, that person needs standing and an effective way to intervene. Fourth, the intervention must change the outcome. We should measure each step separately so we can diagnose the mechanism. A design might improve visibility while worsening correction because people become overloaded. We also need to name whose control we mean. A manager may gain authority while a worker or affected stakeholder loses a way to contest the decision. Measure mistaken vetoes as well as successful ones, and preserve task performance and human effort as separate outcomes. This is a project proposal rather than an established empirical finding.

organizational.title: Three initial comparisons
rows: A person reads and forwards the handoff
A person checks and edits the report
organizational.caption: Hold final human authority and shared-workspace permissions constant initially.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. Begin with these three conditions on the same task family. Keep final execution rights and shared-workspace permissions constant. The inputs can be matched, but the realized messages and human attention will differ, and we should measure those differences rather than claim perfect information matching. The human-relay condition helps separate routing from substantive editing. If mediation improves correction, add a delay-matched direct-collaboration condition to see whether the gain comes simply from slowing decisions. Then study bounded delegated execution in a separate stage. Otherwise, we might attribute the benefit of requiring approval to the topology of communication. This is a staged comparison design. We have not yet selected final task materials, numerical success thresholds, or sample size. Those require feasibility work before a confirmatory study.

organizational.title: Separation can leave important dependencies
items: Common inputs or correlated initialization can align behavior.
Files, tools, and environmental changes can transmit information.
A visible handoff can carry distinctions its reviewer misses.
organizational.caption: Identical software alone does not prove a secret runtime channel.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. The meeting's shared-prior objection is important. Two instances may respond similarly because of common information or dependencies established before the task. That is different from discovering a hidden runtime channel. We should avoid treating shared architecture itself as proof of communication. At the same time, removing direct messages does not establish statistical independence. The feedback proof assumes an existing product form and shows how it is preserved; it does not establish that observation erases arbitrary prior dependence. We must also account for shared artifacts and environmental actions, which can carry information. Finally, a human may forward content without understanding everything it communicates. A routing requirement does not certify comprehension. Sources: meeting transcript, lines 141–169; feedback draft, PDF pp. 24–26. These are qualifications motivating tests, not a claim about any named deployed service's actual data sharing.

organizational.title: Costs and limits of islands
rows: Workload and delay may defeat useful oversight
Assistants may miss contradictions or produce incompatible plans
Summaries may suppress rare or dissenting evidence
Separate assistants may still depend on one provider or gatekeeper
organizational.caption: Coordination quality and individual human agency need separate evaluation.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. A design that makes some actions more predictable may also make the organization less capable. Restricting collaboration can remove useful cross-checking. Human reviewers can become overloaded, especially if a high volume of routine approvals makes the exceptional case harder to notice. Summaries can hide the very disagreement needed for correction. Local separation also leaves questions of ownership, access, and exit. A person might have a nominal veto while lacking the expertise, time, or institutional security to exercise it. These are proposed failure mechanisms to measure, not effects already demonstrated by this research. Sandy's concern in the meeting about beneficial coordination is central here: we want warranted collective action that remains contestable. Source for that discussion: numbered transcript, lines 107–110.

organizational.title: What would support or weaken the hypothesis?
rows: Supports mediation in this task and setting
Weakens the case for requiring mediation
Points toward timing or permission controls
Rare evidence or task quality suffers
Counts against the tested island design
organizational.caption: Proposed tests, with decision criteria specified before the confirmatory study
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. The pilot should have ways to reject our preferred story. Introduce a known error, a changed constraint, or a consequential dissenting signal. Randomize task versions and condition order where feasible. Evaluate successful correction separately from detection, unnecessary vetoes, elapsed time, overall quality, and reviewer effort. After a feasibility pilot, set quantitative thresholds and sample planning before the confirmatory study. A positive result would support a mechanism in that task, not a general claim about society. If direct logged collaboration performs as well, then requiring people to relay everything may be unnecessary. If delay explains the effect, a rate or permission limit may be simpler. If mediation drops rare evidence, the interface needs revision even when average prediction looks good. These are pre-result evaluation criteria.

organizational.title: Conditional policy implications
items: Require reviewed handoffs for the relevant decisions.
Bound delegated actions or change approval timing.
Preserve source access and an exception route.
Protect direct human deliberation and ways to contest authority.
organizational.caption: Candidate governance requirements. Current evidence does not establish a universal communication ban.
organizational.notes: About 90 seconds. These are conditional design proposals that could eventually become organizational requirements. Each should name its mechanism, scope, human cost, and a result that would overturn it. The first three depend on evidence about how a particular workflow fails. The last expresses a value commitment: people should retain meaningful participation and a way to contest authority. Information theory alone cannot choose that commitment. It can help us investigate whether an implementation supports it. We should also distinguish local governance proposals from claims about existing law; this talk makes no legal claim. The strongest current output is a concrete research program: specify the interface, test correction, account for costs, and retain the possibility that direct collaboration with appropriate permissions is better in some settings.

organizational.title: The decision for the research group
organizational.statement: Which mechanism should the first islands experiment isolate?
items: Does a structured report preserve what people need?
Does review arrive early enough to matter?
Can a person make the correction effective?
organizational.notes: Reserve about 5 minutes for discussion, fitting the full presentation into a 20-minute slot. Ask Alec which mechanism is essential to the proposal and what comparison would persuade him to permit a direct AI channel. Ask the group whose corrections should count and which dissenting evidence must survive a report. My suggested first study holds final human authority fixed and compares communication and reporting arrangements. That keeps the mechanism interpretable. Then study delegation separately. These are discussion prompts, not assignments accepted by anyone. Close with the relationship to the first talk: identifying useful organization tells us something about a system's interface, while designing an institution requires deciding who can act through that interface and assessing whether the action works.

organizational.title: Backup: what remains separate
rows: Observation masking and deleting a channel
One changes the observer, the other changes the process
A rank estimate and a human attention budget
Seeing a message and understanding it
Power and justification require separate arguments
organizational.caption: Modeling commitments for the proposed pilot
organizational.notes: Optional backup. These distinctions address the most likely overextensions of the conceptual connection. No general theorem translates a neural PCA dimension into the capacity of a human reviewer. Likewise, a larger joint simplex is an ambient representation budget, not proof that every predictor must store that many coordinates. Simon's notes motivate nonlinear and lookback comparisons. The policy discussion should preserve the useful question about asymmetric understanding while avoiding a single complexity inequality as a safety criterion. Sources: feedback draft pp. 37–38; Simon's Iliad notes pp. 7–10; Alec's working draft sections 2–6, treated as a tentative proposal.
